analysis.one_liner: Blocks EPA from tightening national smog and soot air-quality standards for four years.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 202 cosponsors from both parties, but it never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never got a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered EPA not to issue any new or revised national air-quality standards for ozone (smog) or fine particulate matter (soot) for four years. Instead, EPA would spend up to five years studying the health effects of fine particles and building a fine-particle monitoring network, with grants to states of up to $75 million a year. Only after that review could EPA decide whether the existing standards should stay as they are.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be businesses that emit smog- and soot-forming pollution — especially coal-fired power plants, factories, and refineries — because a four-year freeze on tighter standards would postpone any new pollution-control requirements and the costs that come with them. States and counties facing stricter air designations would also get breathing room. The bill's own text notes EPA's scientific advisers had called for more research on fine particles, which is the stated rationale for waiting.

how_it_helps.text: Bars EPA for four years from issuing any new or revised national ambient air quality standards for ozone or fine particulate matter, keeping the existing, weaker standards in place [S2][S3].

Directs EPA to complete a thorough review of the ozone and fine-particle criteria and standards, including study of health effects, particle sizes retained in the lungs, and the biological mechanisms of harm [S2][S3].
Authorizes EPA to require state fine-particle air monitoring and to make grants to states for it, with up to $75 million per year in appropriations for fiscal years 1998 through 2002 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the cost would fall on people who breathe the air — particularly people with asthma, lung disease, and other respiratory conditions — who would live under older, weaker smog and soot standards for at least four more years while the mandated review ran its course. Under the Clean Air Act, ambient standards are the trigger for pollution controls on power plants, factories, and vehicles, so delaying them delays those controls.

drawbacks.text: A mandatory four-year freeze applies no matter what the science shows in the meantime; the bill's own text acknowledges fine particles can cause adverse health effects whose mechanisms are not yet fully understood [S3].
Delaying new standards would delay the designations and pollution-control programs that follow from them, extending exposure to smog and fine particles linked to respiratory disease [S2][S3].

A good-faith supporter would concede the uncertainty point: more research and monitoring before tightening standards has real value, but the bill locks in the delay for a fixed four years rather than tying it to when the research actually answers the question.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated case — finish implementing the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, gather fine-particle monitoring data, and study health mechanisms before changing standards — is not baseless, and it does fund real monitoring. But a rigid four-year moratorium on standards protects compliance budgets, not lungs: it would postpone whatever controls the eventual science justified, at the cost of years of continued exposure to the old, weaker standards. On balance, the bill's design puts the interests of regulated polluters ahead of the people the Clean Air Act standards exist to protect.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Commerce Committee and its Health and Environment subcommittee from June 1997 until Congress ended in January 1999; even a discharge petition meant to pull it out of committee went nowhere, and the bill never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Ron Klink introduced the bill on June 19, 1997, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce [S1][S5].
A week later it was referred to the subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it remained [S5].

On October 9, 1997, Representative Collin Peterson filed a motion to discharge the committee — a procedure to force a bill out of committee and onto the floor — but the bill never reached the floor [S5].
The bill accumulated 202 cosponsors, 54 Democrats and 148 Republicans, yet the committee never reported it and no chamber ever voted on it before the 105th Congress ended [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Polluting industries were the intended beneficiaries of the moratorium; because the bill died in committee, they got no four-year freeze and EPA's authority to tighten the ozone and fine-particle standards stayed intact. Everyone who breathes the air was spared four more years of the older standards.

for.name: Rep. Ron Klink
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the House floor.

for.name: 202 House cosponsors (54 Democrats, 148 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad bipartisan backing on paper.

for.name: Rep. Collin Peterson
for.what_they_did: Filed a motion to discharge the committee to force the bill toward a floor vote.

for.name: Utility, manufacturing, and refining trade associations
for.role: Industry groups affected by the Clean Air Act's ozone and particulate standards
for.what_they_did: Ran a public campaign in 1997 against EPA's proposed tighter smog and soot standards, the rules this bill would have frozen.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce (Chair John Bliley)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup; it sat in the Health and Environment subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Public health organizations, including the American Lung Association
against.what_they_did: Publicly backed EPA's proposed tighter ozone and fine-particle standards and opposed legislation to delay them.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily bipartisan — 202 members split 54 Democrats and 148 Republicans [S4] — but no chamber vote ever took place, so the record shows bipartisan sponsorship and a quiet death in committee rather than a partisan floor fight.

industries.note: Ozone and fine-particle standards are the legal trigger for pollution controls on power plants. A four-year freeze on tighter standards would have postponed new control requirements and their costs for coal-burning plants, while the public absorbed the health effects.
These industries emit smog- and soot-forming pollution and would have gained years of delay before any stricter standards forced new emissions controls or fuel changes.

industries.industry: State and local air quality agencies
industries.note: The bill authorizes federal grants — up to $75 million a year — for state fine-particle monitoring, which agencies wanted; but the moratorium would also have delayed the attainment designations and planning that flow from updated standards.
